title: The Tidal Tales of NGC 922
caption: The peculiar galaxy NGC 922, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 922 · constellation Fornax · about 140 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Image Processing: J. Miller (International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Rodriguez (International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab) & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: An umbrella-shaped tidal tail spreads out from NGC 922 in this image, a feature only recently detected. The peculiar galaxy lies in the southern constellation Fornax, about 140 million light-years away, and its structure has puzzled astronomers for years.

Its distinctive features, a plume of stars and a galactic bar that sits off-center, were once blamed on a collision, some 330 million years ago, with a dwarf galaxy nearby. The new observations challenge that story. The newly seen tail does not line up with the path of the dwarf galaxy, and the dwarf itself is still forming stars and has a well-defined shape, which does not fit the aftermath of a direct hit.
A newer idea is that NGC 922 may have merged with a stripped dwarf galaxy, one that had already lost much of its material in earlier encounters with other galaxies.
scale: The source lists a distance of 140 million light years, so the light in this picture set out roughly 140 million years ago.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 922 through g, r and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.

understand.eye: The faint tidal tail is far too dim to see by eye. Deep exposures and a z filter reaching into invisible near-infrared light bring it out.

explore: As scientists rewrite the galaxy's history, its tidal features make NGC 922 a valuable case for understanding how galaxies develop after interactions. The image was taken with the DOE-built Dark Energy Camera on the NSF's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.
alt: A distorted galaxy with an off-center bar and an umbrella-shaped tail of stars spreading from it.
